items.title: QUIZ ON QUEENING COMBINATIONS
items.text:
229. White moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing by Black’s King. How does he drive off the blockader and win the game?

230. Black moves. His Passed Pawn is prevented from advancing to the queening-square by White’s Bishop. How does Black get rid of the Bishop?

231. White moves. He is ahead in material and has several ways of winning. The quickest method is to simplify by sacrificing, so that his Passed Pawn can march on irresistibly. How does White accomplish this?

232. Black moves. This position will be recognized as a “relative” of 224. How can Black clear away most of the pieces in order to reach a simplified position in which his Passed Pawn can advance victoriously?

“CASTLE EARLY and often!” is the way one wit put it, to emphasize the necessity of getting the King into safety as quickly as possible.

Of the two methods of castling, the King-side is preferable in the great majority of cases; but even there, the King is not quite secure. He is hemmed in by his own Pawns, and cannot advance; yet, being posted on the first rank, he cannot retreat! It is therefore logical to conclude that the King is vulnerable to checks by Rook or Queen on the critical first rank.

This leads to a very natural question: why not assure the King’s safety by advancing one of the Pawns in front of him, in order to create an escape (a “loophole”) for His Majesty? In the end-game stage, such an advance of one of the Pawns is usually in order. During the middle-game, however, it is inadvisable to disturb the position of the Pawns in front of the castled King. An alteration in the Pawn position creates weaknesses which allow hostile pieces to occupy threatening posts whence they can no longer be driven away by Pawns.

items.title: BASIC PATTERN FOR THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK
items.text:
233A. Black is checkmated. Offhand it might seem that he had been a bit careless and overlooked the mate pictured in the diagram. That this is not the case, can be seen from the next diagram, which shows how this position came about. Later on, we shall see that the weakness of the first rank often makes remarkable combinations possible. Sometimes the result is outright mate, as here; other times, exploitation is indirect.

233B. White moves. Spotting the weakness of Black’s first rank, he plays 1 xa8! The sacrifice is decisive, because it removes one of the defenders of Black’s first rank. After 1 ... xa8 Black has only one Rook guarding his d8, while White has two Rooks trained on it. There follows: 2 d8+, xd8; 3 xd8 mate, as in 233A. In such situations, the creation of a “loophole” by (say) ... h6 is advisable.

234A. Black moves. His Queen and a Rook are trained on White’s first rank, which is guarded by a Rook and Bishop. But the Bishop, being pinned, is paralyzed. Therefore the first rank is vulnerable to attack. Black can invade by sacrificing his Queen: 1 ... e1+! forcing 2 xe1.

235A. White moves. It seems difficult if not impossible to penetrate Black’s first rank. Yet it can be done; and if we look for all possible checks and captures, we find the violent move 1 xd7+! Black plays 1 ... xd7 (1 ... b8 avoids mate but leads to frightful loss of material).

236A. White moves. He attacks the h-Pawn twice, and it is defended only once. Not realizing that his Queen is tied to the defense of the first rank, he plays 1 xh5? With this capture, White’s first rank becomes vulnerable. To prove this, Black sacrifices his Queen with 1 ... xh5! As he cannot remain a Rook down, White retakes: 2 xh5.

234B. Black moves. He recaptures with his Rook, and White is checkmated! Of course White’s Bishop must not interpose.

Since a vulnerable first rank implies mating possibilities, it often permits the most fantastic sacrifices of material. See 244A!

235B. White moves. He continues with occupation of the vulnerable rank: 2 e8+. Black must interpose by 2 ... d8. Now either White Rook captures the Rook, giving checkmate. The brilliant sacrifice 1 xd7+! was perpetrated in actual play by Paul Keres on World Champion Alekhine.

236B. Black moves. He swoops down the whole length of the open file: 2 ... c1+. White interposes with 3 f1; perhaps he overlooks the long-range effect of Black’s Bishop at a6! Black now follows through with 3 ... xf1 mate. (Had White played 3 d1, he would have delayed the mate for one move.) The Queen sacrifice was startling but logical.

237A. Black moves. He wants to invade White’s first rank via the e-file. The play in 235A tells us what to look for. Searching for forcing moves such as checks or captures, Black decides in favor of 1 ... axd2 White recaptures by 2 xd2. (If 2 xd2, xd2; 3 xd2, e1 mate!)

238A. White moves. His Queen and Rook are doubled on the c-file – one of the surest methods of dominating an open line. Such control enables one to use the file as a “jumping-off place” for forcible entry into the hostile position. The opponent’s first rank is a favorite target for this type of attack. White plays 1 g3 with a double threat.

239A. Black moves. It is not clear how he can work up an attack against White’s first rank. But the process of looking for checks and captures again gives us a priceless hint. We begin with 1 ... f3+, which forces White’s King to g1 in order to keep the Rook guarded. Now White’s first rank is vulnerable. The search for checks and captures yields a delightful sequel: 2 ... xf1+!

237B. Black moves. By sacrificing the exchange, he has rendered White’s first rank vulnerable to invasion. Two of the defenders of White’s e1 are gone, so that Black can play 2 ... e1+!; 3 xe1 (or 3 f2, e3 mate), xe1 mate. Black’s first move was an example of removing the guard.

238B. Black moves. His Knight is attacked; hence 1 ... g6, parrying the threat. But White had another threat, made possible by the retreat of the Bishop. This menace, far from obvious, now becomes reality: 2 c8+, xc8; 3 xc8 mate! Black could have avoided this mate, but only at the cost of leaving his attacked Knight in the lurch.

239B. White moves. He has only one reply, 3 xf1, which is resoundingly answered by 3 ... d1 mate. Black’s Pawn at f3 acts as a powerful wedge (actually doing the work of a Bishop or Queen) in blocking the escape of the White King. All of Black’s moves were violent: the more stringently the defense is limited, the easier it is to foresee the consequences.

240A. White moves. He begins with 1 c4+ (1 b3+ has the same effect), which is as strong as it is obvious. Strong because it drives Black’s King into the corner, which makes his first rank vulnerable; obvious because all checks and captures are obvious – they must be the first moves one looks at. Black is forced (why?) to play 1 ... h8. Now comes the brilliant 2 f7!

241A. White moves. He plans to drive Black’s King into the corner. As in 240A, Black’s King will have no mobility – no space to move freely if checked. Knowing what to look for, White plays the brilliant 1 xg7+! Black replies 1 ... xg7 (1 ... h8 allows mate in two – how?). The play continues 2 f7+, h8.

242A. White moves. He plays the “brilliant” move 1 xf6?, reckoning on 1 ... gxf6; 2 xf6+ and mate next move. But, by removing his Rook from the first rank, White has weakened that line. Black reasons that if the other Rook disappears, the vulnerable first rank will be open to mating threats. This leads to the forcing 1 ... xa1!

240B. Black moves. There is no adequate defense to the threat of 3 xg7 mate. If Black plays 3 ... xf7; 4 xe8+ forcing mate next move on the vital rank. 3 ... g8 guards the mate, but 4 xe8 has catastrophic consequences for Black. The chief cause of Black’s downfall is the uselessness of his Queen. Successful attack or efficient defense is difficult without the Queen.

241B. White moves. His brilliant next move should be seen in a flash – look for checks and captures! Black’s first rank, guarded only by a Rook, is attacked by White’s Queen and Rook. How can this concentrated menace be utilized? Answer: 3 f8+! xf8; 4 xf8 mate. Four consecutive checks, two of them captures, led to Black’s downfall.

242B. White moves. Threatened with mate or disastrous loss of material, he is resigned to his fate. He Plays 2 xa1, allowing 2 ... xd1+ and mate in two more moves.

When the Rooks are disconnected, as in 242A, there is often a likelihood that the first rank will be vulnerable to attack.

243A. White moves. He has two attacking “batteries”, the Queen, Bishop and f-Pawn operate against g7; the Rooks control the only open line. To obtain the cooperation of all these forces, he uses a discovered attack: 1 xd7!, xd7; 2 f6! (This Pawn has been unpinned by the sacrifice of the exchange.)

244A. Black moves. He must not snatch at the Queen: 1 ... xb7??; 2 xe8+, xe8; 3 xe8 mate – vulnerable first rank! Instead, Black plays the startling but logical 1 ... xe2! making use of the same weapon to checkmate White! After 2 xe2 White’s first rank is vulnerable. Black proves this immediately as his Rook whizzes down the open file: 2 ... c1+.

245A. White moves. His first observation is that Black’s Rooks are disconnected – always a likely indication of a weak first rank. But White’s goal is not mate; he sees that he can only force the win of a piece. After 1 xb4, xb4; 2 d2 there is a double attack menacing the Rook at b5 and also threatening 3 d8+, xd8; 4 xd8 mate.

243B. Black moves. He is confronted with two threats: 3 xd7 or 3 fxg7+, which wins at least a Rook. To parry both threats, he is forced to play 2 ... fd8. But White wins anyway: 3 xd7! After 3 ... xd7 Black’s first rank is denuded of defenders. He is helpless against the deadly Rook move: 4 e8 mate.

244B. White moves. He cannot stave off mate, but he has a venomous last trap. If he tries 3 e1, then 3 ... xe1+; 4 xe1, xe1 mate. Instead, White plays 3 e1, inviting the blunder 3 ... xe2?? when 4 b8+ (or 4 a8+) forces checkmate on Black! But Black is wary: he plays 3 ... xe1+! 4 xe1, xe1 mate. These witty possibilities deserve careful study.

245B. Black moves. He realizes that if he retreats his Rook from attack, he will be mated as shown. So he defends both threats with 2 ... e7. White plays 3 d8+ just the same. He sees that he will win a piece. Black interposes with 3 ... f8 (not 3 ... xd8??; 4 xd8 mate) and now White wins a piece with 4 xf8+, xf8; 5 d8+ (double attack!)

items.title: QUIZ ON THE VULNERABLE FIRST RANK
items.text:
246. White moves. What is the quickest way to remove the guardian of Black’s first rank, making the Black King vulnerable to mate next move?

247. White moves. He cannot force mate, but he can make use of the vulnerable first rank idea to queen his Passed Pawn. How? (Hint: see 221B.)

248. White moves. His situation is apparently critical, for if he plays 1 d6 (forced?) there follows 1 ... xe1+; 2 f2, e4+. Yet White can win by exploiting Black’s vulnerable first rank. How?

249. White moves. Black’s Bishop is paralyzed and prevents the Rook from guarding the first rank. How can White win material by taking advantage of the weakness of Black’s first rank?

WE HAVE SEEN how a piece which is attacked may be won, by making life miserable for its defender. The protector is either destroyed, removed by exchange, or driven off. In all such cases, the defensive function comes to an end.

When these methods of gentle persuasion fail, another effective device is still available. This is to interpose a piece (or force the enemy to do so!) which interferes with the flow of force leading from the piece under attack to its protector. The life-giving current is shut off; the threatened piece is stranded and left to its fate.

Pieces which do not have effective contact with their own forces (such as a Knight stranded at the edge of the board) are particularly susceptible to a break in communications. In general, beware of time-wasting captures which require a piece to travel far afield.

items.title: BASIC PATTERN FOR BREAKING COMMUNICATION
items.text:
250A. Black moves. His powerful pressure against the h-Pawn is neutralized by White’s Queen. Black breaks the line of communication by 1 ... d3!!

250B. White moves. If he plays 2 xd3, Black continues 2 ... xh3+; 3 g1, g2 mate. Or if 2 xd3, xd3; 3 xd3, d6+ (double attack!) and wins.

251A. Black moves. His Bishop attacks White’s Knight, which is protected by his Rook. The Rook cannot be driven off, nor threatened with capture or exchange. Yet its protective power can be nullified by 1 ... d2+, forcing 2 c1.

251B. Black moves. He still attacks the Knight, but it is no longer guarded by the Rook. The line of communication has been snapped by the forced retreat of White’s King. Consequently Black wins easily by simply removing the Knight: 2 ... xe1.

252A. Black moves. He plays to win a Pawn, without realizing that he will be breaking the line of communication that guards a vital piece. He captures by 1 ... gxf4 and after 2 gxf4, he snatches the seemingly undefended Pawn by 2 ... xf4?

252B. White moves. His Queen attacks Black’s Queen, which is protected by a Rook. He severs the line of communication with 3 g3+. If now 3 ... f7, Black’s Queen has lost the protection of the Rook, so that 4 xf4+ wins at once.

253A. White moves. He pins and doubly attacks Black’s Bishop at e7, which is doubly defended. To drive away Black’s Queen from the defense, White plays 1 f4. Now Black cannot play 1 ... xf4?? (removal of the guard) because of 2 xe7 mate. Or, if 1 ... f6, the skewer 2 g5 makes the pin decisive. Black therefore tries 1 ... c5.

253B. White moves. He plays 2 d6, striking for the third time at the pinned Bishop, which is overwhelmed, as it is attacked three times and defended only once. The d-Pawn has added its weight to the attack; but more important is the fact that it has wedged itself between Bishop and Queen, cutting their line of communication. Black is lost; if 2 ... cxd6; 3 xe7 mate.

254A. Black moves. He can win a piece, but how? His Rook at b2 attacks the Bishop, which, however, is defended. How can Black break the line of communication when there is no line of communication?! The answer is: by creating such a line! Thus: 1 ... d5. White replies 2 e8, for if 2 c4, b5 wins a piece by double attack! (Retreat by the Bishop to d3 or e2 was of course impossible.)

Black has separated the Queen and Bishop, yet the Queen still exercises protection from a4 to e8.

254B. Black moves. With the venomous Pawn push 2 ... b5, he breaks the line of communication, attacking the Queen and winning the Bishop. Creating a line of communication in order to break it is a novel device! There is an analogy in the story of the preacher who was exhorting his congregation to repent, and save themselves from the lot of sinners in the Hereafter – where “There will be weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth.” “Suppose I have no teeth?” an old lady asked. “Teeth will be provided,” was the preacher’s quick reply.

ON THE CHESSBOARD, surprise is nothing more than logic that packs a wallop. The impact of surprise thrills the perpetrator, pleases the kibitzer, crushes the victim.

Many years ago, the distinction was subtly established by the famous lexicographer who was caught (by his wife, of course) in the act of kissing the maid.

“Why, John!” his wife exclaimed, “I’m surprised!”

Even in this trying situation (which might be described as the basic pattern for the surprise move), the dictionary-compiler’s training did not desert him.

“You’re not surprised,” he answered. “I’m surprised. You’re astonished.”

Chess is so prolific in the variety of combinations it produces that it may seem pointless to isolate a certain kind of move and call it a “surprise” move.

We have already been taught to “expect the unexpected.” No matter how brilliant a move may be, it cannot startle us if it is also the logical move – the move that conforms to the pattern of the combination we are seeking.

Yet there are times when a move is so wildly fantastic that it jolts us out of our seats – until we realize that for all its bizarre appearance, it is earnestly sane and carefully evaluated. Such a move, which ruthlessly rips away the superficial aspects of the position, may rightfully be called a “surprise” move.

For the audience witnessing a game between experts, a surprise move has the thrill an unexpected knockout gives to fight fans watching two evenly matched prize fighters. For the reader of master games, a surprise move gives more joy than seven miles of painfully correct analysis. The surprise move has all the delicious quality of a witty remark lighting up a learned discourse.

When do such moves occur? Usually at the beginning of a combination: a piece is given up to smash the hostile King’s position by a mating attack. But often the surprise move can be played with incomparably greater effect as the last in a series of innocuous moves or exchanges, in a position which seems completely harmless.

This second course is a great favorite with the modern master, who finds it highly effective, because less hackneyed, to wind up his combination with a stinging surprise.

It may seem out of place to give advice on how to guard against surprise moves, when the greatest masters have at one time or another succumbed to their electrifying effect. But the habit of examining every possible check or capture will reduce your losses.

The positions which follow may be studied with profit, but their chief purpose is to delight the reader with their fireworks effects. As for the victims of surprise moves, they may agree with Caesar, who, when asked which sort of death was the best, said: “That which is unexpected.”

255A. Black moves. He invades enemy territory by 1 ... e2, threatening 2 ... xf2 mate or 2 ... xf2 mate. It is relatively best for White to make a temporary escape with 2 h3, with a prosaic loss in prospect. But he instinctively guards the weak spot with 2 f1?

256A. White moves. He has given up a piece for a strong attack, which is all the more virulent because Black’s Queen is cut off from the defense. For his concluding combination, he has prepared a charming sacrifice. He plays 1 g7+ forcing 1 ... f7. And now the sur prise: 2 e6+!!

257A. White moves. How can his Queen participate in the attack with no loss of time? To avoid giving Black a breathing spell, White plays 1 b5! Black must do something about his Queen – at once! Therefore he has no time to attend to his King’s welfare. Black replies 1 ... xb5 (other Queen moves allow the same continuation).

255B. Black moves. He has a surprise move: 2 ... xf3! White captures by 3 gxf3, whereupon Black gracefully winds up the White King’s career with 3 ... g6 mate – an “epaulet” mate! The White Rooks which hover so anxiously around their King actually bring about his downfall!

256B. Black moves. Rocked on his heels by the unexpected Queen sacrifice, he has no choice but to accept: 2 ... xe6. The capture is answered by 3 dxe6 mate! Despite the army of White pieces trained on Black’s King, it remained for the not-so-humble Pawn to deal the death -blow!

257B. White moves. His clever Bishop sacrifice cleared the way for action by the Queen – but not at once (2 h5??, f1 mate!). Again time is of the essence – another violent move is needed: 2 xh7+!, forcing 2 ... xh7. Now White mates by 3 h5+, h6; 4 xh6 mate. “Surprise is nothing more than logic that packs a wallop.”

258A. White moves. Threatened with mate on the move, he hits on the superb surprise move 1 b6+!! Pundits would analyze this fearless plunge into a nest of hostile Pawns as a Knight fork, based on a pin (Black’s c-Pawn is paralyzed), plus a sacrifice as a clearance for the White Queen. But for our purposes the Knight move is a magnificent stroke, too delightful to desecrate by dissection!

259A. Black moves. He sees the three-move threat of mate with 1 h7+, f8; 2 e6+, fxe6; 3 xg7 mate. What more natural than 1 ... xd4 parrying the threat and winning a piece? But Black gets a rude awakening, as White replies with the electrifying 2 h8+.

260A. Black moves. He plays 1 ... e3. This attacks the Queen. If 2 xe3?? xg2 mate. If White retreats his Queen from attack, then 2 ... xg3; 3 xg3, xg3 with a piece ahead.

But White thinks he sees a way out: gaining time with a check, he will remove one of the Rooks and then pin the dangerous Queen: 2 xg6+, fxg6; 3 c4.

258B. Black moves. He captures: 1 ... axb6. Utilizing the open a- file, White replies 2 a8 mate. (Black could have avoided the mate by moving his King in reply to 1 b6+!! – but this would have meant losing the Queen.)

This is a perfect example of the value of studying every possible check or capture.

259B. Black moves. He has no choice: he must play 2 ... xh8, allowing 3 xh8 mate. The Queen sacrifice seems a lot less startling to one who is familiar with mating patterns (see the section on that subject). An early combination by Dr. Euwe, who later became World Champion.

260B. Black moves. Apparently White has defended with genuine skill. He has avoided the loss of a piece, and he is about to exchange Queens. True, Black can now win by 3 ... xc4; 4 xc4, d3 and 5 ... d1. But at least White will be losing creditably.

Instead, Black mates on the move: 3 ... xh3 mate! The pinned Queen is still pinning!

261A. White moves. He is the exchange ahead – enough to win, but there is no obvious immediate decision. However, White has a beautiful surprise move which gives Black his quietus: 1 d5!!, offering his Rook in four different ways! Despite these alternative ways of capturing, the White Rook is anything but vulnerable.

262A. Black moves. Since White’s King cannot move, mate can be administered by any Black checking piece safe from capture. This is the logical explanation of the extraordinary play that follows: 1 ... xb2!! threatening 2 ... xh2 mate. If now 2 h3, h2 or if 2 h1, e1, forcing mate in either case. White prefers to be “shown.” He plays 2 xb2, which is answered by the stunning 2 ... e5!!

263A. Black moves. He begins with 1 ... xh3! relying on a Knight fork (if 2 gxh3? the family check 2 ... f3+ wins at once). But White has a resource: counterattack with 2 c5.

Black (Marshall) plays 2 ... g3!!! The Queen must be taken, as 3 ... xh2 mate is menaced.

261B. Black moves. Which way does he want to be mated? If 1 xd5; 2 f6 mate (overworked Queen). If 1 ... xd5; 2 f8 mate (vulnerable first rank). Finally, if 1 ... exd5 or 1 ... xd5; 2 xd8 mate (breaking communications)! Nor can Black really refuse the Rook, as 2 xd8 mate and 2 xd4 are threatened.

262B. White moves. Life is still very difficult for him, the threat being 3 ... g6 mate! He has no alternative but to play 3 fxe5. But now the real blow descends, for Black’s earlier sacrifices, brilliant though they were, served only as preliminaries. Black plays 3 ... g5 mate! It was the fatal position of the White King that made the surprise moves logical.

263B. White moves. His opponent has just played the most brilliant move in the history of chess! White is helpless: if 3 hxg3, e2 mate! If 3 fxg3, e2+; 4 h1, xf1 mate. Or 3 xg3, e2+; 4 h1, xg3+; 5 g1, e2+ with a piece ahead. So White resigns. “Some of Marshall’s most sparkling moves look at first like typographical errors” (Napier).

THERE HAS NEVER BEEN a good definition of the word “combination.” We can come close to the real meaning by saying that a combination is a series of forcing moves which result in checkmate, gain of material, or improvement in position. In a combination we impose our will on the opponent by forcing his replies.

The patterns that we have studied so far – the pin, the Knight fork, the double attack, the discovered check and the rest, are all fundamental; they form the basis of combination play.

When we combine two or more of these themes – say a pin followed by a Knight fork – we are on the way to understanding and playing combinations on a grand scale, the kind that mark the play of a master. Combinations which at first sight may seem difficult to understand, become clear and simple when broken down into their component parts. The amazing combinations of Alekhine, Keres, Capablanca and the other great masters can be reduced to basic elements that we know and understand from our study of the preceding chapters.

What these masters create on the chessboard may be compared appropriately to the full stage presentation of the master magician. The layman is bewildered by the overpowering procession of illusions. The magician’s colleagues, on the other hand, see in his performance “nothing more” than a grand combination of familiar themes. The sleight-of-hand, the shuffling and concealment of cards, the palming of coins, the disappearing goldfish, the woman sawed in half – all these are only the equivalent of the chess master’s bag of tricks: the pins, Knight forks, double attacks and discovered checks.

There is one important distinction between the magician and the chess master. When the layman discovers how illusions are created, there is a great psychological let-down. When the chess student is given a rational explanation of the mechanics of chess combination, his enjoyment of the game is intensified.
